title: Fitting exterior featheredge timber cladding
subtitle: Fix overlapping softwood featheredge boards to an exterior timber-frame or masonry wall
excerpt: How to fit featheredge timber cladding to an exterior wall. Covers fixing horizontal battens, setting out the board spacing, cutting and fixing the boards with stainless nails, and treating the finished cladding.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK timber cladding trade practice.

glossaryTerms.definition: A softwood cladding board, typically 150 mm wide, tapered from a thick bottom edge (about 12 mm) to a thin top edge (about 3 to 5 mm). Boards overlap each other by about 25 to 30 mm to throw water clear. Standard UK exterior cladding material, also called bevel siding or bevelled cladding.

A horizontal batten fixed to the wall face before the cladding boards are nailed on. The battens create a drained and ventilated cavity behind the cladding and provide a nailing line for each board. Battens are typically 50 x 25 mm softwood fixed at the same spacing as the board exposure (the vertical distance between each board's top edge and the one below).

fixed horizontally to the wall, creating a ventilated cavity behind the cladding. The setting-out calculation ensures even spacing between boards from the sill to the soffit.

Fix 50 x 25 mm pressure-treated softwood battens horizontally to the wall face at the calculated board spacing (typically 115 to 125 mm centres for 150 mm wide boards). On a timber-frame wall, screw the battens into the frame members. On a masonry wall, plug and screw at 600 mm intervals. Use the spirit level to check each batten is level before tightening. Fit a vertical strip of breather membrane or DPC over the wall below the battens on masonry walls to prevent water bridging into the wall through any nail or screw holes.

Measure the height from the bottom of the wall to the soffit line. Divide this by the number of boards needed to fill the height at an overlap of 25 to 30 mm. Adjust the exposure (the visible face of each board) until the spacing comes out even, with the top board sitting neatly under the soffit. Mark a story rod (a length of batten marked with the actual board positions) to transfer the spacing consistently across the wall.

At the base of the wall, fix a narrow packing piece of the same thickness as the thick edge of the featheredge board (about 12 mm) along the bottom batten. This tilts the first board out at the same angle as all subsequent boards. Nail the starter board thick edge down to the bottom batten with two 65 mm stainless steel annular-ring nails per board width. Check level.

Rest each board on the thick edge of the board below and align to the story rod mark. Nail through the thick lower edge of the incoming board (not through both boards; nailing through two boards locks their movement and causes splitting as the timber moves). Use one nail per batten crossing, keeping the nail at least 25 mm from the thin top edge of the board. Cut boards to length with the crosscut saw at internal and external corners; use a 45-degree mitre at external corners or an external corner trim batten.

Apply exterior wood treatment, stain, or paint to the completed cladding and to the end grain of all cut boards before the cladding is exposed to weather. End grain soaks up water fastest. Retreat every two to four years depending on the product used and the exposure of the wall.

attrs.symptom: Boards cupping and pulling away from the battens
attrs.cause: Boards were not treated before fitting, allowing moisture to enter the exposed back face.
attrs.fix: Treat both faces and all edges of replacement boards before fitting. Stainless annular-ring nails resist pull-out better than plain-shank nails.

attrs.cause: Nail positioned too close to the end of the board, or standard round-wire nails used instead of oval nails or annular-ring nails.
attrs.fix: Pre-drill pilot holes within 50 mm of board ends. Use 65 mm stainless oval or annular-ring nails which split the grain less than round wire nails.
